question: When model size and training horizon are co-scaled along a compute-optimal ladder, do normalized loss trajectories converge to a scale-independent curve, why does learning-rate decay make cross-scale differences fall below seed noise, and can collapse diagnose bad scaling choices?

key_findings.claim: Within each tested scaling ladder, subtracting a fitted irreducible loss and normalizing compute and each realization's final reducible loss produces strikingly aligned training curves.
key_findings.evidence: The normalized curve is ell(x,p,omega)=[L(x t*(p),p,omega)-L0]/[L(t*(p),p,omega)-L0]. Transformers span roughly 10M-80M parameters by width 768-2048 at fixed depth three on grayscale CIFAR-5M pixels and Lichess characters; seven-layer MLP widths 384-2048 fit a synthetic power-law Fourier target. Curves align within a task/schedule, not onto one common curve across tasks or schedules.

key_findings.claim: The paper's 'compute-optimal' label primarily means a fitted training horizon, not joint optimization of all scale-dependent hyperparameters.
key_findings.evidence: Five-seed constant-learning-rate loss curves define a compute-loss Pareto frontier; a power law c*(p)=kappa p^(1+gamma) is fit after dropping smallest/largest-model outliers, using c=6tp. The resulting t*(p) is reused for decay schedules under an assumption of constant-factor optimality. Width/depth, batch size, weight decay, schedule shape, and most architecture choices are not jointly optimized.

key_findings.claim: Supercollapse is partly a real cross-scale regularity and partly an intentional variance-reduction construction tied to the observed final loss.
key_findings.evidence: By definition every normalized curve equals one at x=1 and collapse deviation Delta(1)=0. Elsewhere the denominator uses the same stochastic trajectory's final loss, exploiting time-correlated noise as a control variate; with decay, Delta falls below the raw per-model relative noise sigma for as much as roughly the last half of training. Normalizing by expected rather than realized final loss would remove this below-noise effect.

key_findings.claim: Two selected misscaling interventions visibly break collapse before strongly degrading endpoint scaling, supporting sensitivity but not yet a validated diagnostic.
key_findings.evidence: For the synthetic MLP, replacing muP learning-rate scaling with one constant learning rate across widths disrupts normalized trajectories. For chess, changing the fitted data exponent from 1.02 to 1.2 produces a systematic size-dependent shift. Each ladder receives a separate best-fit L0, and no preregistered threshold, held-out ladder, false-positive rate, or comparison against endpoint-based model selection is reported.

anchors.section: 2.6 Suboptimal Scaling Breaks Supercollapse and Figure 4

key_findings.claim: For an exact two-term sum of power laws, compute-optimal balance and exact trajectory collapse are algebraically equivalent up to a constant training-horizon factor.
key_findings.evidence: With L=L0+t^-mu+p^-nu, optimizing allocation at fixed compute gives mu t^-mu=nu p^-nu and t*(p) proportional to p^(nu/mu). Substitution cancels every p dependence in the normalized curve, leaving [r x^-mu+1]/[r+1]. Constant-learning-rate CIFAR and MLP/chess curves are approximately fit by this form after early transients are omitted.

key_findings.claim: The general theorems sharply qualify collapse as a unique certificate of compute optimality.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem E.1 proves full collapse implies a power-law Pareto frontier only under smoothness, a continuum of interior optima, and the chosen affine normalization; power-law frontier gives merely first-order agreement near the forced endpoint. The appendix acknowledges zero-ending schedules put the optimum on a boundary. For multi-term laws, compute optimality yields asymptotic collapse, but the converse fails, constant multiples of t* also collapse, and a single dominant term can cause trivial collapse under suboptimal exponents.

anchors.section: E Power-Law Pareto Frontier is Necessary
Remarks on converse and trivial collapse

key_findings.claim: The learning-rate-schedule model treats SGD noise as a perturbation around schedule-independent gradient flow and predicts excess loss from learning rate times a preconditioned gradient-covariance trace.
key_findings.evidence: For quadratic loss the expected loss splits into a noiseless forcing term and a convolution of eta Sigma over Hessian modes; an adiabatic late-time approximation gives excess loss about one quarter eta Tr(Sigma). The nonlinear appendix derives a first-order small-noise analogue with a time-varying Hessian and, for Adam, a slowly varying preconditioner.

anchors.section: 3.2.1 A Simple Model for LR Schedules

key_findings.claim: The quantitative schedule prediction is a fitted reconstruction using statistics from the target trajectory, not a zero-run forecast of an unseen training schedule.
key_findings.evidence: A single coefficient alpha=0.21 for CIFAR and 0.26 for MLP is fit while predicted target loss uses delta eta times Tr(Sigma') measured on a fixed 2M-token set from the target run. Thus the method can reconstruct how loss changes across schedules and scales after obtaining target covariance, but compute savings and out-of-sample schedule prediction are not established by this experiment.

anchors.section: 3.2.2 Predicting Loss Curves Across Schedules and Figure 6

key_findings.claim: Several theoretically inconvenient effects are empirically absorbed or omitted, so the SGD-noise account is explanatory rather than identified.
key_findings.evidence: The paper fits alpha away from the nominal one-quarter coefficient, leaves unexplained why Tr(Sigma)/reducible loss scales in cross-entropy with non-negligible irreducible loss, drops eta Tr(delta Sigma) because including it can worsen fits, and assumes a fixed/slow Adam preconditioner despite its dependence on stochastic gradients. The limitations also exclude finite-step edge-of-stability effects and schedule-dependent deterministic trajectories.

anchors.section: Effect of Dropping eta Tr(delta Sigma) and Figure 13

key_findings.claim: The empirical universality claim is a small-scale proof of concept with architecture- and data-specific universal functions, not a demonstrated large-model universality class.
key_findings.evidence: The largest primary Transformer is about 80M parameters with three blocks, CIFAR is repeatedly reused beyond one epoch, Lichess data ordering is fixed in most experiments, and depth scaling shows only a decent collapse with an unexplained shift. The discussion explicitly calls large-scale and realistic co-scaling of width, depth, batch, weight decay, and other factors future work.

anchors.section: Training for More than One Epoch
B Scaling Collapse Across Transformer Depths

method.core_idea: Estimate a compute-optimal token horizon for every model size, normalize both elapsed compute and reducible loss by their final values, quantify residual cross-model variation against seed noise, and explain the resulting collapse with power-law balance plus a perturbative SGD-noise model.
method.mechanism: At compute-optimal allocation, leading time- and size-dependent power-law loss terms have equal scale, so normalization cancels parameter-count dependence. Learning-rate schedules expressed in normalized time deform all model sizes similarly if preconditioned gradient covariance divided by loss is scale-universal. Dividing by each realization's final loss cancels correlated stochastic fluctuations; decay reduces noise accumulated between any late time and the endpoint, yielding supercollapse.
assumptions: Expected loss curves are well approximated after transients by a finite sum of power laws in training tokens and parameter count.
A fitted irreducible loss L0 is meaningful and transferable within each scaling ladder and schedule.
Training FLOPs are proportional to 6tp and parameter count p is the relevant size coordinate.
A power-law fit to a five-seed Pareto frontier reliably estimates t*(p) after endpoint outlier removal.
Horizons optimal for constant learning rate remain optimal up to a constant under decay schedules.
muP or the chosen depth multiplier makes deterministic dynamics and curvature statistics comparable across scale.
Gradient noise is a small perturbation around a schedule-independent gradient-flow trajectory with slowly varying Hessian and covariance.
Adam's preconditioner changes slowly and can be treated as fixed between deterministic and stochastic paths.
Tr(preconditioned Sigma)/loss is approximately a function only of normalized compute for a fixed schedule.
Time-correlated seed noise dominates model-to-model normalized-curve differences in the studied ladders.

techniques.role: Fits a power-law compute-optimal horizon from constant-learning-rate multi-seed loss curves.
Subtracts fitted irreducible loss and normalizes each stochastic trajectory by its own final reducible loss.
Measures relative variance of normalized curves jointly over model sizes and seeds.
Compares collapse deviation with per-model raw reducible-loss variation across seeds.
Derives scale cancellation from compute-optimal balance of time and model terms.
Models schedule effects through gradient-flow time and learning-rate-scaled gradient covariance.
Measures Adam/muP noise magnitude in transformed coordinates on a fixed token sample.
Tests constant cross-width learning rate and an overlarge data exponent as negative controls.

evaluations.setting: Three-block muP Transformers of about 10M-80M parameters autoregressively modeling grayscale CIFAR-5M pixels
evaluations.metric: Compute-loss Pareto frontier, normalized loss curves, collapse deviation Delta, per-model seed noise sigma, and fitted scaling law
evaluations.result: Strong collapse under constant learning rate and below-noise supercollapse through much of the decay phase for multiple schedules
evaluations.baseline: Raw loss curves, wrong irreducible-loss offsets, and constant-learning-rate noise floor

evaluations.setting: Character-level three-block Transformers on Lichess with width and separate depth ladders
evaluations.metric: Final scaling law and normalized-curve alignment
evaluations.result: Width scaling supercollapses near the fitted gamma=1.02 horizon; gamma=1.2 breaks alignment; depth scaling has a visible residual shift
evaluations.baseline: Over-trained data exponent and width-versus-depth scaling

evaluations.setting: Seven-layer MLPs of widths 384-2048 fitting a synthetic power-law Fourier target
evaluations.metric: Loss scaling, normalized collapse, and schedule reconstruction
evaluations.result: muP scaling supercollapses and the covariance-trace model fits schedules with alpha=0.26; a constant learning rate shared across widths disrupts collapse

evaluations.setting: CIFAR and MLP target schedules reconstructed from constant-learning-rate reference runs
evaluations.metric: Predicted versus observed loss curves over schedule, size, and horizon
evaluations.result: Equation 16 tracks curves with alpha=0.21 or 0.26 when target-run covariance trace is supplied
evaluations.baseline: Reference loss plus learning-rate-only change; the dropped covariance-change term sometimes worsens fits

evaluations.setting: Exact and fitted two-/multi-power loss models
evaluations.metric: Analytical p-independence and finite-size collapse error versus data exponent
evaluations.result: Compute-optimal balancing yields exact two-term or asymptotic multi-term collapse; small exponent errors can visibly separate finite curves
evaluations.baseline: Perturbed data exponents and nonzero offset errors

limitations: Primary Transformers are only about 10M-80M parameters and three blocks; no billion-parameter language-model pretraining ladder is tested.
Each dataset and learning-rate schedule has its own universal curve, so universality means within-ladder scale invariance rather than one cross-domain function.
Compute optimality chiefly covers the training horizon and does not jointly optimize architecture, batch size, weight decay, schedule, or all hyperparameters.
The irreducible-loss offset is fitted separately and collapse quality is sensitive to it.
Endpoint normalization forces exact agreement at x=1 and exploits final-loss noise; supercollapse is not independent validation of endpoint predictability.
The negative-control evidence contains only two selected misscaling mechanisms and no calibrated out-of-sample diagnostic benchmark.
The necessary-collapse theorem assumes interior optima and does not directly cover zero-ending schedules used in the experiments.
Power-law frontier is only first-order sufficient, multi-term collapse has non-unique/trivial converses, and any constant multiple of optimal horizon preserves asymptotic collapse.
The schedule predictor requires target-trajectory covariance statistics and fitted alpha, limiting its prospective compute-saving interpretation.
The perturbative theory omits finite-step EoS, schedule-dependent deterministic paths, and Adam preconditioner feedback.
Including the covariance-change term can worsen fits, and cross-entropy covariance scaling with irreducible loss remains unexplained.
CIFAR and some Lichess models reuse data for multiple epochs, and fixed Lichess data ordering narrows the seed-noise sources.
No downstream capability, calibration, robustness, or representation metric is shown to share the loss-curve collapse.
failure_modes: A wrong fitted L0 can create or destroy apparent collapse even when raw trajectories are unchanged.
Endpoint normalization can hide systematic final-scale errors and guarantees Delta=0 at the endpoint.
A suboptimal ladder dominated by one loss term can collapse trivially, producing a false positive.
Several data exponents can balance different terms in a multi-power law, so best collapse need not identify the unique compute-optimal exponent.
Finite-size ladders can make a wrong exponent look better or worse depending on the sampled model range.
Schedule-specific alpha or unmeasured covariance change can invalidate loss-curve transfer to an unseen schedule.
Large-step EoS dynamics can change the deterministic path rather than merely inject noise, breaking the SDE deformation model.
Adam preconditioner changes can couple scale, schedule, and noise in ways not captured by a fixed transformed covariance.
Data exhaustion, multi-epoch memorization, tokenization, or architecture changes can alter the Pareto frontier outside the measured ladder.
A smooth loss collapse can coexist with scale-dependent capability emergence or safety behavior.
reusable_insights: Use complete normalized trajectories, not just endpoints, to diagnose inconsistent scaling across model sizes.
Always report how fitted offsets and per-realization endpoint normalization contribute to a claimed collapse.
Compare collapse deviation with both seed noise and held-out predictive error; below raw noise can arise from a control variate.
Treat collapse as a necessary-consistency clue rather than a unique optimality certificate unless false positives are ruled out.
Separate horizon optimality from full configuration optimality in scaling-law language.
Measure target-free predictors if the intended application is to avoid running expensive schedules; target-run covariance reconstruction is a different task.
Test collapse across width, depth, batch, weight decay, data mixture, optimizer, and architecture under a genuinely co-scaled ladder.
Audit whether capabilities and internal mechanisms collapse along with loss before asserting a universal training dynamics class.
open_questions: Does pre-registered collapse quality predict the optimal data exponent on held-out larger models better than endpoint Pareto fitting?
What false-positive collapses arise from single-term dominance, wrong offsets, data reuse, or endpoint normalization?
Can schedule effects be predicted without running the target schedule or measuring its gradient covariance?
Does supercollapse persist at billion-parameter scale with realistic depth, batch, weight decay, data mixture, and optimizer co-scaling?
Is there one cross-domain universality class after additional rescaling, or are universal curves intrinsically task and schedule specific?
Do gradient norms, curvature, representation change, and downstream capabilities collapse on the same normalized time coordinate?
Can an EoS-aware or central-flow model explain the fitted alpha and the failure of the covariance-change term?
How should uncertainty in L0, gamma, and frontier extraction propagate into collapse confidence intervals and deployment decisions?

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Kaplan et al. fit endpoint loss against parameters, data, and compute over broad ranges and derive compute allocation. The target paper normalizes entire trajectories and uses within-ladder collapse as a more sensitive consistency diagnostic, but at much smaller Transformer scale.

competitive_landscape.title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Hoffmann et al. train over 400 models from 70M to 16B parameters and validate near-equal model/token scaling with a 70B model. The target paper studies whole-curve invariance on 10M-80M proxies and fits only the horizon as compute-optimal, without a comparable large-scale confirmation.

competitive_landscape.title: Reconciling Kaplan and Chinchilla Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.difference: Pearce and Song explain discrepant exponents through parameter counting and finite-scale bias and recommend total parameters/compute. The target paper assumes c=6tp and uses a narrow ladder; its trajectory collapse could complement, but does not replace, those accounting and scale-range audits.

competitive_landscape.title: 4+3 Phases of Compute-Optimal Neural Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.difference: Paquette et al. solve an infinite-data SGD model and derive optimizer-noise, capacity, and feature-embedding phases plus exponents. The target paper uses the resulting multi-power intuition to explain empirical trajectory collapse and adds schedule/noise observations, but takes the relevant power laws as given.

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling Law with Learning Rate Annealing
competitive_landscape.difference: Tissue, Wang, and Wang fit an explicit law using accumulated learning-rate and annealing areas to predict full curves from one or two runs across schedules. The target paper derives an SDE-inspired covariance-trace correction and focuses on cross-scale collapse, but needs target covariance measurements rather than offering the same direct low-run prediction claim.

competitive_landscape.title: A Multi-Power Law for Loss Curve Prediction Across Learning Rate Schedules
competitive_landscape.difference: Luo et al. empirically fit multi-power terms across observed schedules, predict unseen shapes/horizons, and optimize a schedule beyond cosine. The target paper gives a simpler noise-based deformation that explains collapse, but its own appendix notes a constant-covariance variant underperformed and it does not optimize schedules prospectively.

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling Exponents Across Parameterizations and Optimizers
competitive_landscape.difference: Everett et al. train tens of thousands of models up to 26.8B parameters, compare optimizers/parameterizations, and show non-muP prescriptions can transfer or outperform muP. The target paper treats muP as its main width-consistency mechanism and tests one deliberately constant learning-rate failure, leaving broader parameterization equivalence unexamined.

competitive_landscape.title: Small-scale proxies for large-scale Transformer training instabilities
competitive_landscape.difference: Wortsman et al. reproduce large-scale instabilities in high-learning-rate small models and use activation/gradient scaling to forecast failures. The target paper proposes normalized loss-curve collapse as a finer general scaling diagnostic, but has not validated its decisions against actual larger-model outcomes.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Compute-optimally trained neural networks exhibit universal normalized loss dynamics, with learning-rate decay producing below-noise supercollapse; power-law balance and SGD noise explain the effect, and collapse can diagnose scaling choices more sensitively than endpoints.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper documents within-ladder collapse across two Transformer datasets and a synthetic MLP, provides negative scaling controls, proves exact/asymptotic cancellation for power-law families, and connects below-noise alignment to endpoint control-variate normalization and schedule-dependent noise.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Whole-trajectory scaling collapse and its explicit variance-reduction account are a useful and relatively clean contribution. 'Universal' must be narrowed to a task- and schedule-specific curve across small models under a fitted horizon and offset. Collapse is not uniquely diagnostic of optimality, and the schedule model is reconstructed using target covariance. A follow-up brief would be generic scaling-law/prospective-diagnostic work and substantially duplicate existing prospective-criticality, EoS-allocation, and scaling-oriented flagships; no new brief is justified by this cluster.
